newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 25.

text.p: Police officers throughout New Zealand were said to be shellshocked on Sunday at the revelation that the fellow officer they had raised $11,000 for had been charged with faking an attack by a Satan-worshipper. Page 1.

Tighter immigration requirements have cost New Zealand more than $400 million in investment, tourism and education spending by Taiwanese in the past year, according to an immigration consultant. Jimmy Wong, of Southern Skies Consultants, Taipei, said New Zealand Immigration Service figures showed a drop of 97 percent in immigration from Taiwan in the past year. Page 1.

The future of Jim Bolger as head of New Zealand's government was touched on at talks he held with Apec leaders on Sunday, his first day in the Philippines, before Monday's summit of leaders of 18 Pacific Rim countries. Bolger met with Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong to discuss their commitments to the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation goal of free trade by 2010 for developed countries. Talks with Apec leaders so far have focused on the broad Apec vision of free trade. Bolger has been discussing investment moves and new membership of the bloc. Page 2.

Fraud could be costing the insurance industry $50 million a year, AMI Insurance chief executive John Balmforth says. He said AMI had been affected by fraud in key areas such as contents insurance and vehicle insurance. "The phenomenon is not new, but the increasing incidence of deliberate and organised fraud is of real concern," Balmforth said. Page 17.

Sealord's export licences for European Union and North American markets have been reinstated, the Nelson-based fishing company says. The licences were suspended two weeks ago when Sealord failed a European Union and Agriculture Ministry inspection. Page 19.

Air New Zealand is considering selling its airline catering business. Air NZ spokesman David Beatson said on Sunday the possible sale was not related to "Project Save", the airline's campaign to cut $100 million of spending, but was part of an asset management project looking at how to get the best value from parts of the company. Page 19.
New Zealand's largest bank, a combined Trust Bank and Westpac Bank, will be called Westpac Trust. Groups which included hundreds of customers were formed to choose the name. Page 19.
Economic development and the creation of wealth are possible only when government and businesses work together, Foreign Affairs and Trade Minister Don McKinnon has told Apec ministers. Page 19.

Insurance investigators examining the burned-out house of Palmerston North detective Brent Frederick Garner played a key role in events leading to his arrest for allegedly faking his brutal attack. Garner, now facing forgery, arson and false pretences charges, sparked a large manhunt after saying an attacker tied him up, cut crosses in his back, doused him in petrol and set the house on fire on October 18.

The final phase of coalition talks started on Sunday, with a blunt warning from a key Labour negotiator that NZ First leader Winston Peters risks rage among his supporters if NZ First makes a deal with National. In his regular Sunday News column, former Labour Prime Minister Mike Moore abandoned the political niceties surrounding the talks to give NZ First the warning.

NZ First released a detailed paper on Sunday on its compulsory superannuation savings scheme to counter mounting criticism from the Council of Trade Unions and the Alliance. The eight-page paper includes an explanation of why New Zealand needs a savings vehicle to deliver its independence from foreign investment. As well as maintaining national superannuation, NZ First wants to introduce a compulsory savings scheme from July 1 next year, the contributions starting at three percent of income and rising to eight percent by the year 2002.

NZ First continues to cop flak from disaffected long-time workers unhappy at the influence of former MP and strategist Michael Laws. The party's former Canterbury regional chairman Ross Gluer is the latest to throw in the towel. Also reported as having resigned is Terry Hefferman who has been with NZ First since its inception, while former finance spokesman and Nelson candidate Bernard Downey is reportedly considering his future.

Citibank has emerged as a clear winner in an Employers Federation survey of bank charges for small business. The survey indicates that Citibank offers savings of more than 30 percent over its competitors.

Buffeted by surging imports and stagnant exports, New Zealand's trade deficit with Australia has breached the A$2 billion barrier to add new fuel to concern about the strength of the Kiwi dollar. Australian Bureau of Statistics figures show Australia's trade with New Zealand grew by 41 percent in the year ended September, pushing up the surplus to $2,036 million.

A survey of expectations released by the Reserve Bank shows the New Zealand dollar and interest rates are expected to fall next year. The survey conducted by MRL Research on November 6 showed that overall monetary conditions were perceived to have loosened since the last survey in August and they were expected to loosen further by the end of March 1997.
